sentences.text: Canada's distinctive role in the Allied Industrial Base is as a resource and processing anchor: it ranks first among allies on resource & processing positions, and 21 economies count it as their best-placed trusted partner somewhere in the chain.
That role is allied before it is national: at home, uranium mining reads Watch, and battery and EV mineral mining, where Canada holds only 1% of world supply, read Partner.

Its industrial effort should go into batteries, where it makes cells and packs and holds a supplier role in nickel chemicals, and into gas-turbine and drilling components, where it holds a top-quarter position.
The fence that matters is narrow: the rare-earth chain, to be secured with allied partners, and the control software of its cells and packs.
Only gas networks need faster deployment, and recorded protection should shift away from steps the strategy leaves open.

The rare-earth chain from refining to traction magnets, where China holds 94% of world supply and trusted suppliers only 4% (shares that battery materials refining repeats); and the battery-management and communications software of cells and packs.
The answer is qualified trusted supply built with allies, stocks until it qualifies and phased limits on adversary sources, and trusted-source rules for the software, not self-sufficiency.
Preserve battery cells and packs and gas-turbine and drilling components.
Catch Up in battery materials refining, on its export share of refined battery materials; build EV manufacturing on committed investment and extend gas turbines and LNG plant.
Keep uranium, nickel chemicals and aluminium wire rod reliable for allies: an allied commitment, not a domestic fence.

Battery and EV minerals from trusted producers such as Australia and the United States; rare-earth and wind materials from Germany, Belgium and Spain, where allied supply falls short; coal-plant components from allied makers; solar-grade polysilicon.
With developing partners, add trusted capacity in rare-earth and wind materials and in batteries, through project preparation, development finance and offtake.
Accelerate gas networks, buying equipment competitively from trusted suppliers, and build storage, grid, wind and solar on a market footing.
Leave open wafers and PV cells, grid metals refining and grid components, and gas liquids processing.
In Figure 1, Partner sits in battery and EV minerals, coal-plant components and wind materials refining, and Catch Up fills most manufacturing columns, including nuclear refining and fuel.

Orange corner flags mark the High-fence parts inside other steps, the traction magnets and the battery control software; grey flags mark Watch layers, such as grid and turbine control software, inside Catch Up steps.
Each cell is a supply-chain step of a technology, colored by its strategic choice.
A corner flag marks a mixed step whose named parts sit behind a different fence: in EV drivetrain components, the traction magnets are Secure and the step Catch Up.
A dotted outline marks a review case, a call resting on low confidence, a review flag, a thin anchor or a known data artifact; this brief does not turn those calls into recommendations.

Secure is a narrow call for Canada: one whole step and three layers inside other steps, which form two capabilities.
The rare-earth chain: separation, metals and magnets
Feeds the traction magnets of EV motors.
The refining step also covers battery metals; Canada holds 1% of its world supply and <1% of world exports.
China holds 94% of world supply and trusted suppliers 4%; it provides 38% of Canada's imports, and rebuilding takes more than three years.
New trusted separation, metal and magnet capacity with allies such as Japan, Australia and the United States, through co-investment and offtake, and at home where a foothold can be built.
Stocks until it qualifies; adversary-source limits in critical uses, phased in.
Battery-management firmware, energy-management software and communications gateways can command, update or disable Canada's cells, packs and storage from abroad.
China holds 55% of world supply of cells and packs and provides 36% of Canada's imports; the data do not measure who supplies the software.

A trusted-source requirement for firmware, communications and remote access; certification, testing and continuous monitoring; restrictions on over-the-air updates by untrusted vendors, applied to Canadian and imported packs alike.
The magnets of blades, towers and nacelle parts read Catch Up there but Secure in EV drivetrains; this brief treats both as the same chain.
Of control software, only the battery layers sit behind the fence: grid, inverter, turbine and vehicle control layers read Watch.
Their hardware shares are modest (for example, 22% of PV module and inverter imports), and the data do not measure who supplies the software.
Medium fence — where industrial capability matters
Here Canada makes its real industrial choices: is a capability worth having (Strategic Industrial Value), and how strong is Canada today (Competitive Position)?
Most of its 13 Catch Up steps rest on small shares of world supply in mixed trade codes, so this brief builds on few.
Battery cells and packs is the strongest Preserve call: a top-quarter position (87) on operating capacity, with high value (97).
With 1% of world supply, keeping the position means expanding it.
Gas-turbine and drilling components also clears the bar, on a top-quarter position (77), high value (73) and moderate confidence.
Reactors and steam generators read Preserve on low confidence, and oil production is flagged for review by the engine, so both are review cases.
Battery components rests on three anchors, including committed investment, with a position of 71 and high need (70), but the call carries low confidence, so it is a review case.
Battery materials refining has high confidence but a single anchor, 6% of world exports, and a position of 0: a trade position to build from, not proven refining capacity.
The AIB's share of nickel intermediates and chemicals (10%) corroborates the nickel side, not lithium, cathode or anode materials.
EV and charger manufacturing adds committed investment to small trade shares, from a low position (25).
Gas turbines and LNG plant (65) extends an existing position with high confidence.
In transformers, switchgear and cables, whose value just clears the bar, the case sits in large power transformers, power conversion and HVDC control.
EV drivetrain components starts from a position of 46, so it is a build with allied partners.
Other Catch Up calls are weaker than they look, and this brief does not build on them:
Uranium conversion and enrichment: a supply share (3%) that more likely reflects uranium compounds, concentrate included, than conversion capacity; the enrichment layers inherit it.

Nuclear fuel and reactor parts: a basket that mixes reactor and fuel lines with generic boiler and steam-turbine parts; reactors and steam generators, on similarly mixed codes, read Preserve on low confidence, a review case.
Wind turbines and their parts: positions of 36 and 39 in trade codes dominated by cables, transformers and switchgear, with towers that include transmission masts.
PV modules and inverters: moderate confidence, Watch modules, and trade codes that include chip-making machines.
Battery recycling: an export share (19%) of battery waste, scrap and residues.
Drilling rigs, tankers and oil equipment: a value at the bar (60) and low confidence, a review case.
Battery and EV mineral mining have very high need (89), but their value is capped below the bar because it rests on market size alone.
Source them deliberately from trusted producers such as Australia and the United States; allied supply covers the need.

Coal-plant components read Partner on high need and low value: contracts with allied makers such as Japan, South Korea and Italy should suffice, on weak partner evidence; coal-plant equipment reads Watch.
Solar-grade polysilicon is a Partner layer.
Rare-earth and wind materials refining reads Partner on high need (74); allied supply falls short, so the answer is offtake and co-investment with Germany, Belgium and Spain.
